problems.question: A counter reads 25 counts a minute with nothing in front of it and 25 with a rock sample in front of it. What does that tell you about the rock?

options.label: It gives off no radiation the counter can find
Its nuclei decay only when it is warm

problems.explanation: The 25 counts are background radiation from rock, air and space. A sample that adds nothing to the empty count gives off no radiation the counter can find.

problems.question: A radioactive sample counts 3,000 a minute at 20 °C. It is heated to 500 °C. About what will it count?
problems.explanation: Heat makes the atoms move faster but does not reach the nucleus, so the nuclei decay as often as before and the count stays about 3,000.

problems.question: A source counts 2,000 a minute with nothing in front, 1,950 behind paper, and 30 behind 5 mm of aluminium. The background is 25. What does it give off?
problems.explanation: Paper barely changed the count, so there is no alpha; aluminium brought it down to about the background, so what passed paper was beta, with no gamma left over.

problems.question: Between two charged plates, which radiation bends toward the negative plate, and only a little?
problems.explanation: Alpha particles are positive, so they are pulled toward the negative plate, and they are over 7,000 times as heavy as an electron, so they turn only a little.

problems.question: Radium-226 (atomic number 88) gives off an alpha particle. Which nucleus is left?
problems.explanation: An alpha particle carries away mass number 4 and atomic number 2: 226 − 4 = 222 and 88 − 2 = 86, which is radon.

problems.question: Carbon-14 (atomic number 6) gives off a beta particle. Which nucleus is left?
problems.explanation: In beta decay a neutron becomes a proton and an electron leaves: the mass number stays 14 and the atomic number rises to 7, nitrogen.

worked.title: Counting the steps of a decay series
worked.setup: Neptunium-237 (atomic number 93) decays in a series that ends on bismuth-209 (atomic number 83). Find how many alpha and beta decays it takes.

steps.say: By how much does the mass number fall?
steps.hint: Subtract the end's mass number from the start's.

steps.say: How many alpha decays is that?
steps.hint: Only alpha decay changes the mass number, by 4 each time.

steps.say: What atomic number would 7 alpha decays alone leave?
steps.hint: Each alpha decay lowers the atomic number by 2.

steps.say: How many beta decays bring it up to 83?
steps.hint: Each beta decay raises the atomic number by 1.

worked.finish: Only alpha decay changes the mass number, by 4 each: the fall in mass number counts the alphas, and the betas make up the atomic number.

problems.question: Sodium-24 has 11 protons and 13 neutrons; the only stable sodium has 12 neutrons. Which decay will sodium-24 undergo?
problems.explanation: It holds one neutron more than the stable sodium, so it sits above the band; beta decay turns a neutron into a proton and brings it onto magnesium-24, a stable nucleus.

problems.question: Why do heavy stable nuclei hold more neutrons than protons?

options.label: Every proton pushes on every other, and neutrons add the strong nuclear force's hold without adding any push
Neutrons have a charge that cancels the protons'
Protons slowly turn into neutrons as an atom ages
A nucleus needs as many neutrons as electrons

problems.explanation: The push between protons grows with every pair of them, but the strong nuclear force holds only touching nucleons, so a big nucleus needs extra neutrons to stay together.

problems.question: A sample of phosphorus-32 (half-life 14.3 days) counts 2,400 per minute. About what will it count 43 days later?
problems.explanation: 43 days is three half-lives of 14.3 days, so the count halves three times: 2,400 → 1,200 → 600 → 300.

problems.question: Two samples of the same isotope, one of 1 g and one of 10 g, are watched. Which loses half of its nuclei first?
problems.explanation: Radioactive decay is first order: each nucleus has the same chance of decaying in any day, so the half-life is the same whatever the amount, and temperature does not change it.

worked.title: Dating a wooden beam
worked.setup: A wooden beam from the Fifth's works counts 3.8 carbon-14 counts per minute per gram; living wood counts 15.3. Carbon-14's half-life is 5,730 years. Find the beam's age.

steps.say: What fraction of the living count does the beam keep? (as a decimal, three places)
steps.hint: Divide the beam's count by the living count.

steps.say: How many halvings leave about a quarter?
steps.explain: Half of a half is a quarter: 2 halvings.

steps.say: How old is the beam, in years?
What is carbon-14's rate constant, per year? (three significant figures, in scientific form like 1.21e-4)

worked.finish: Each half-life halves the count: count the halvings, then multiply by the half-life.
